framework_Q: New Classical / Real Business Cycle macroeconomics
p_statement: Aggregate demand shocks (spending, monetary, financial) are a major source of business-cycle fluctuations.
q_statement: Business cycles are driven mainly by real shocks, especially technology (productivity) shocks.
x_title: Endogenous Technology Adoption and R&D as Sources of Business Cycle Persistence
x_claim: A significant part of the post-Great-Recession productivity slowdown was an endogenous response to the demand contraction.
x_evidence: "Our main finding is that a significant fraction of the post-Great Recession fall in productivity was an endogenous phenomenon, suggesting that demand factors played an important role in the postcrisis slowdown of capacity growth."
y_title: Entry, Exit, Embodied Technology, and Business Cycles
y_claim: Shocks to embodied technological change are a significant source of US economic fluctuations.
y_evidence: "Looking at the entry and exit of plants provides new evidence supporting the hypothesis that shocks to embodied technological change are a significant source of economic fluctuations."
p_sources: Summers 1986, Some Skeptical Observations on Real Business Cycle Theory, FRB Minneapolis QR (10.21034/qr.1043); Mankiw 1989, Real Business Cycles: A New Keynesian Perspective, JEP
q_sources: Prescott 1986, Theory Ahead of Business-Cycle Measurement (10.1016/0167-2231(86)90035-7); Kydland & Prescott 1982, Time to Build and Aggregate Fluctuations, Econometrica (10.2307/1913386)
conjunction: The Great Recession depressed productivity through weak demand [Anzoategui et al. 2019], and shocks to embodied technology are a significant source of business fluctuations [Campbell 1998].
conjunction_anon: The Great Recession depressed productivity through weak demand [A], and shocks to embodied technology are a significant source of business fluctuations [B].
x_background: Demand shocks drive the cycle and even measured TFP responds endogenously to demand (K4, K3).
y_background: Exogenous technology shocks are the primary driver of fluctuations (N6).
why_conflict: In one web TFP is an effect of demand-driven cycles; in the other it is the exogenous cause of them. Both cannot be the main story.
orphan_conclusion: Measured TFP can be treated as an exogenous driver of recessions even though it falls in response to them.
llm_notes: Check that Campbell's claim is read as 'primary driver'; 'significant source' alone is compatible with K4.

framework_Q: New Classical / Real Business Cycle macroeconomics
p_statement: Money is non-neutral in the short run: monetary policy changes real output and employment.
q_statement: Monetary factors play little role in business cycles; money is approximately neutral.
x_title: Real Rigidities and the Non-Neutrality of Money
x_claim: Real rigidities combined with small nominal frictions create substantial monetary non-neutrality.
x_evidence: "But this paper shows that substantial nominal rigidity can arise from a combination of real rigidities and small nominal frictions."
y_title: Real Business Cycles
y_claim: Business-cycle comovements arise from optimizing agents with rational expectations and no frictions, money or government.
y_evidence: "Our explanation is entirely consistent with (i) rational expectations, (ii) complete current information, (iii) stable preferences, (iv) no technological change, (v) no long-lived commodities, (vi) no frictions or adjustment costs, (vii) no government, (viii) no money, and (ix) no serial dependence in the stochastic elements of the environment."
p_sources: Romer & Romer 1989, Does Monetary Policy Matter? A New Test in the Spirit of Friedman and Schwartz, NBER Macro Annual
q_sources: King & Plosser 1984, Money, Credit, and Prices in a Real Business Cycle, AER
conjunction: Small nominal frictions combined with real rigidities generate large real effects of money [Ball & Romer 1990], and business-cycle comovements arise in an economy with no frictions and no money [Long & Plosser 1983].
conjunction_anon: Small nominal frictions combined with real rigidities generate large real effects of money [A], and business-cycle comovements arise in an economy with no frictions and no money [B].
x_background: Nominal rigidity makes money non-neutral in the short run (K1, K5).
y_background: Markets clear without frictions, and money plays no role in cycles (N1, N10).
why_conflict: The first web needs frictions and non-neutral money to explain fluctuations; the second explains them while denying both.
orphan_conclusion: Central banks can smooth output fluctuations without welfare cost even though those fluctuations arise in a frictionless economy.
llm_notes: Reads as 'cycles have both monetary and real sources'. Long-Plosser signals its framework, so it is less hidden than the fiscal pairs.

framework_Q: New Classical / Real Business Cycle macroeconomics
p_statement: Money is non-neutral in the short run: monetary policy changes real output and employment.
q_statement: Only unanticipated monetary shocks affect real output; anticipated money is neutral.
x_title: The Timing of Monetary Policy Shocks
x_claim: Output responses to monetary shocks depend on their timing within the year, because wage contracts are staggered unevenly.
x_evidence: "We propose a potential explanation for the differential responses based on uneven staggering of wage contracts across quarters."
y_title: Cross-Regime Evidence of Macroeconomic Rationality
y_claim: Across 47 countries, real output effects of monetary shocks fall as monetary variance rises, as rational-expectations misperception models predict.
y_evidence: "Rational expectations macromodels predict that the short-run effects of monetary shocks on real output (X) should be negatively related across policy regimes to the variability of such shocks."
p_sources: Fischer 1977, Long-Term Contracts, Rational Expectations, and the Optimal Money Supply Rule, JPE (10.1086/260551)
q_sources: Sargent & Wallace 1975, 'Rational' Expectations, the Optimal Monetary Instrument, and the Optimal Money Supply Rule, JPE (10.1086/260321); Lucas 1972, Expectations and the Neutrality of Money, JET (10.1016/0022-0531(72)90142-1)
conjunction: The real effects of monetary shocks depend on when in the year they occur [Olivei & Tenreyro 2007] and shrink in countries with more volatile monetary policy [Kormendi & Meguire 1984].
conjunction_anon: The real effects of monetary shocks depend on when in the year they occur [A] and shrink in countries with more volatile monetary policy [B].
x_background: Staggered nominal wage contracts create the real effects (K1, K5).
y_background: Real effects arise only from unanticipated money via price-level misperceptions in clearing markets (N4, resting on N1, N2).
why_conflict: The mechanisms are incompatible: contract rigidity vs misperception with market clearing. The listed conflict is K5-N4, but the deeper clash is K1-N1.
orphan_conclusion: Monetary policy's real effects vanish when policy is anticipated, yet depend on the staggering of pre-set wage contracts.
llm_notes: Surface claims are both 'money has real effects that vary'; the hidden conflict is about why.

framework_Q: New Classical / Real Business Cycle macroeconomics
p_statement: Debt-financed tax cuts raise consumption and aggregate demand, because many households are liquidity-constrained or not fully forward-looking.
q_statement: Ricardian equivalence holds: replacing taxes with debt leaves private spending and aggregate demand unchanged.
x_title: Household Expenditure and the Income Tax Rebates of 2001
x_claim: Households spent 20-40 percent of the 2001 tax rebates on nondurables within three months, with substantial effects on aggregate demand.
x_evidence: "Households spent 20 to 40 percent of their rebates on nondurable goods during the three-month period in which their rebates arrived, and roughly two-thirds of their rebates cumulatively during this period and the subsequent three-month period." "Consistent with liquidity constraints, responses are larger for households with low liquid wealth or low income."
y_title: The Ricardian Approach to Budget Deficits
y_claim: Budget deficits do not raise real interest rates or lower national saving; debt and tax finance are approximately equivalent.
y_evidence: [Not in abstract. The paper defends Ricardian equivalence (abstract: 'the alternative theory that is associated with the name of David Ricardo'); verify in the body, which argues households offset deficits by saving.]
p_sources: Campbell & Mankiw 1989, Consumption, Income, and Interest Rates: Reinterpreting the Time Series Evidence, NBER Macro Annual (10.1086/654107)
q_sources: Barro 1974, Are Government Bonds Net Wealth?, JPE (10.1086/260266)
conjunction: Households spent much of the 2001 tax rebates, with substantial effects on aggregate demand [Johnson, Parker & Souleles 2006], and budget deficits do not raise real interest rates or depress national saving [Barro 1989].
conjunction_anon: Households spent much of the 2001 tax rebates, with substantial effects on aggregate demand [A], and budget deficits do not raise real interest rates or depress national saving [B].
x_background: Many households are liquidity-constrained or not fully forward-looking, so debt-financed rebates raise consumption (K10).
y_background: Households fully offset deficits by saving more (N9).
why_conflict: If rebate recipients spend the money, private saving does not rise to offset the deficit, so national saving falls; Barro's claim needs the opposite.
orphan_conclusion: Debt-financed tax rebates raise consumer spending at no cost to national saving.
llm_notes: Johnson et al. explicitly test the permanent income hypothesis, but the cited claim (rebates were spent) does not signal it.

x_claim: After the 2001 tax rebates, consumer spending rose, most for liquidity-constrained consumers.

framework_Q: New Classical / Real Business Cycle macroeconomics
p_statement: Government spending multipliers can exceed one, especially with slack or at the zero lower bound.
q_statement: Government spending crowds out private spending, so spending multipliers are at most about one.
x_title: Fiscal Policy in a Depressed Economy
x_claim: At the zero lower bound with hysteresis, expansionary fiscal policy is likely self-financing.
x_evidence: "In a depressed economy, with short-term nominal interest rates at their zero lower bound, ample cyclical unemployment, and excess capacity, increased government purchases would be neither offset by the monetary authority raising interest rates nor neutralized by supply-side bottlenecks." "Then even a small amount of hysteresis—even a small shadow cast on future potential output by the cyclical downturn—means, by simple arithmetic, that expansionary fiscal policy is likely to be self-financing."
y_title: The Ricardian Approach to Budget Deficits
y_claim: Budget deficits do not raise real interest rates or lower national saving; debt and tax finance are approximately equivalent.
y_evidence: [Not in abstract. The paper defends Ricardian equivalence (abstract: 'the alternative theory that is associated with the name of David Ricardo'); verify in the body, which argues households offset deficits by saving.]
p_sources: Christiano, Eichenbaum & Rebelo 2011, When Is the Government Spending Multiplier Large?, JPE (10.1086/659312)
q_sources: Baxter & King 1993, Fiscal Policy in General Equilibrium, AER
conjunction: At the zero lower bound, debt-financed fiscal expansion is likely self-financing [DeLong & Summers 2012], and budget deficits do not crowd out national saving or raise real interest rates [Barro 1989].
conjunction_anon: At the zero lower bound, debt-financed fiscal expansion is likely self-financing [A], and budget deficits do not crowd out national saving or raise real interest rates [B].
x_background: Government purchases raise output more than one-for-one when output is demand-determined and there is slack (K3, K7).
y_background: Ricardian equivalence: replacing taxes with debt leaves demand unchanged (N9).
why_conflict: Conflict holds only if Barro's view is taken to include N12 (spending multipliers at most one). Barro 1989's claim depends on N9, and Ricardian equivalence alone is compatible with spending multipliers above one.

llm_notes: Downgraded after splitting N9 from N12. Looks like a strong pair but the backgrounds may not actually conflict: a useful hard case.

x_claim: Uncertainty shocks produce business-cycle comovements only when prices are sticky, and are worse at the zero lower bound.
x_evidence: "When prices are flexible, uncertainty shocks are not capable of producing business cycle co-movements among key macro variables." "With countercyclical markups through sticky prices, however, uncertainty shocks can generate fluctuations that are consistent with business cycles."
y_title: The Dynamic Effects of Neutral and Investment‐Specific Technology Shocks
y_claim: Neutral and investment-specific technology shocks account for a large share of business-cycle variation in hours and output.
y_evidence: "The neoclassical growth model is used to identify the short‐run effects of neutral technology shocks, which affect the production of all goods homogeneously, and investment‐specific shocks, which affect only investment goods."
p_sources: Summers 1986, Some Skeptical Observations on Real Business Cycle Theory, FRB Minneapolis QR (10.21034/qr.1043); Mankiw 1989, Real Business Cycles: A New Keynesian Perspective, JEP
q_sources: Prescott 1986, Theory Ahead of Business-Cycle Measurement (10.1016/0167-2231(86)90035-7); Kydland & Prescott 1982, Time to Build and Aggregate Fluctuations, Econometrica (10.2307/1913386)

x_background: Sticky prices are required for the result (K1, K4).
y_background: Technology shocks identified within the neoclassical growth model dominate (N6).
why_conflict: If technology shocks explain 44-80 percent of output variation, demand-type shocks cannot be a major source; and Fisher's identifying model assumes flexible prices.
orphan_conclusion: Technology shocks drive most output variation, yet offsetting demand-type uncertainty shocks is the central stabilization task.
llm_notes: Fisher's dependence on N1 runs through the identifying model only; verify.

framework_Q: New Classical / Real Business Cycle macroeconomics
p_statement: Markets, in particular the labor market, need not clear in the short run; involuntary unemployment exists.
q_statement: Employment fluctuations are voluntary, reflecting intertemporal substitution of labor; there is no involuntary unemployment.
x_title: Downward Nominal Wage Rigidity, Currency Pegs, and Involuntary Unemployment
x_claim: Downward nominal wage rigidity under currency pegs causes involuntary unemployment; capital controls can cut it by about 5 points.
x_evidence: "We document that nominal wages are downwardly rigid in emerging countries." "The model predicts that the combination of a currency peg and free capital mobility creates a negative externality that causes overborrowing during booms and high unemployment during contractions."
y_title: Intertemporal Labor Supply and Human Capital Accumulation*
y_claim: The intertemporal elasticity of labor supply is much higher than conventional estimates once human capital accumulation is modeled.
y_evidence: "We solve and estimate a dynamic model that allows agents to optimally choose their labor hours and consumption and that allows for both human capital accumulation and savings." "Estimation results and simulation exercises indicate that the intertemporal elasticity of substitution is much higher than the conventional estimates and the downward bias comes from the omission of the human capital accumulation effect."
p_sources: Keynes 1936, The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money, ch. 2 (involuntary unemployment)
q_sources: Lucas & Rapping 1969, Real Wages, Employment, and Inflation, JPE (10.1086/259559)
conjunction: Downward nominal wage rigidity under currency pegs causes involuntary unemployment [Schmitt-Grohe & Uribe 2016], and the intertemporal elasticity of labor supply is much higher than conventional estimates [Imai & Keane 2004].
conjunction_anon: Downward nominal wage rigidity under currency pegs causes involuntary unemployment [A], and the intertemporal elasticity of labor supply is much higher than conventional estimates [B].
x_background: Involuntary unemployment from wage rigidity (K1, K2).
y_background: High intertemporal substitution, the basis of voluntary employment fluctuations (N7).
why_conflict: K2 says unemployment is involuntary; N7 says employment fluctuations are voluntary substitution.
orphan_conclusion: Cyclical unemployment is a voluntary response to temporarily low wages, and reducing it through devaluation raises welfare.
llm_notes: Imai-Keane supports N7 but does not claim cycles are voluntary; dependence is indirect.
